A potentially groundbreaking highlight hidden in the @CMSGov 2027 PFS is also this gem:

A formal request for information (RFI) to overhaul or eliminate the CPT coding system, specifically floating the ideas of using ICD10-PCS to establish payment or using broader categories (similar to how DRGs work for inpatient).

A quick history lesson on CPTs:

-The @AmerMedicalAssn created CPTs in 1966 to standardize medical billing terminology, which otherwise didn't exist at the time.

-In 1983 then-CMS (known as HCFA) made CPTs (as HCPCS) the required code set for Medicare Part B

-In 1992, the AMA created the RUC which is a committee of different specialties that recommend to CMS the RVU values for each CPT. CMS generally took the recommendation, until recent years it started layering in other data to augment it.

-In 1996 HIPAA mandated standardizing electronic transactions and CPT was the required code set for any platform doing physician billing.

The @AmerMedicalAssn makes the majority (55-60%) of their revenue from royalties licensing the CPT code set. Every EHR, billing software vendor, hospital, practice, and payer that processes a claim pays to license the codes — and CMS itself pays to use CPT in Medicare billing. The government mandates the codes... and the AMA collects the licensing fees.

This monopoly has been criticized by @RFKJrHealthSec @SenBillCassidy @RepJamesComer and others...so it feels like this little section II.H in the 2027 CMS PFS is a very interesting move by the Administration to potentially completely revamp healthcare billing...

Quick lay person guide to aortic dissections:

-the aorta is THE vessel that carries blood from your heart to the rest of the body

-its walls can split and “dissect”, creating a false lumen for blood to divert in

-the “flap” can block flow to important places (arms, brain, etc.) and cause ischemia

-it can also dissect into the pericardium and cause blood to fill around the heart (cardiac tamponade)

-treatment is open heart surgery, a stent (TEVAR) and/or medical management of your blood pressure and heart rate, depending on the Type (A or B)

-fatality is extremely high if unmanaged 

-symptoms: severe, sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and/or ischemia symptoms like weakness/pain in limbs or stroke like symptoms.

911, every time.

To add to the sordid tale of healthcare and private equity, check out this oxymoron:

Private Equity + Nonprofit.

Seems antithetical to one another, but here we are.

Rather than buy a nonprofit hospital outright, PE buys the control, leaves the nonprofit shell (and tax benefit) standing, and calls ot joint venture. It's an acquisition without triggering the regulation of acquisitions. 

Fast facts from @PEstakeholder's killer new report on it:
~500 healthcare facilities now operate as nonprofit-PE joint ventures. 

-These avoid State AGs and the FTC regulations because they either don't have traditional asset sales or nonprofit conversions (State AGs) or are individually each too small for FTC review

-Besides slashing patient care and heightening profits, there's some other usual financial hacks like the sale-leaseback of hospital real estate. Cash out now, generate a payout that can fund a dividend, pay rent forever. 

-The IRS rules governing all of this were written in 1998 and 2004 — well before PE poured $1 trillion into U.S. healthcare

There’s little as American as obesity and little as AmericanHealthcare as paying for complications instead of prevention…

Obesity costs us at least $260 billion a year in healthcare dollars. And it’s proven to cause downstream morbidity and mortality: coronary disease, diabetes, joint issues…

Finally, @MedicareGov decided to pay for prevention by funding GLP1s for obesity before the complications happen…but it’s only for 20 months as part of “The Bridge” plan. 

It’s hard to be a real plan, though, if there is no solution after 20 months…at best, a concept of a plan…

Read more from me on @Medscape 

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/obesity-dilemma-pay-now-or-pay-what-it-becomes-later-2026a1000lo1

Don’t get me wrong, I think AI scribes are incredible —but I also think in our excitement to use it, we skirted over some important details and now the lawsuits are here.

Consent is essential and needs to be documented (and not autopopulated/hard coded into the note like one system being sued allegedly did). 

Education on how doctors should be consenting patients is absolutely abysmal. It isn’t “hey, I’m going to use this ai scribe on my phone, is that cool?” — that’d be like consenting to a surgery with “hey, I’m going to remove your organ, is that cool?”

Consent needs risks, benefits and alternatives discussed. Problem is, the doctors using AI scribe platforms aren’t being told everything they need to know to consent…Is the patient’s voice saved or just the transcription? For how long? Is it identifiable? Is it sensitive? What about the voice/words of their family/friend in the room? What about the hallway patient within voice-range or the consultant/nurse at the nearby desk? What’s the security on the data being saved? Have there been breaches? Who owns the data after it leaves servers and what can it be used for (can it be sold? Used for training?Can it be subpoenaed?) What’s the laws in your state (1 party consent or 2 party consent) to be recorded?

Without knowing these answers, my opinion is it’s hard to truly consent. The misfire here isn’t using AI scribes, it’s skirting over the legalities of patient consent. 

Read more from me at @Medscape:

https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/first-do-no-harm-then-press-record-2026a1000ire

@EdGainesIII has a great thread on the new CMS rule for IDR

It always amazes me how little people, doctors included, know about the No Surprises Act (NSA) and IDR (independent dispute resolution).

The TLDR is NSA banned physician groups from billing patients when physicians were out of network and insurances wouldn’t pay. Awesome and the right thing for patients, but then the legislation forced physician groups to recoup money from insurances via forced arbitration (IDR) with very high fees. Even if you won, it was still 6-12mos+ to get any cash in the bank...but the fees and cost get paid upfront…

CMS just issued their updated rule on IDR, which dropped one of those fees by 87%, from $230 to $30. As an aggregate, this drop represents over $500M in fees.

Good news, but obnoxious, since if insurances would just pay physicians in the first place, then the fees wouldn’t exist at all. Cheaper arbitration is still arbitration...

Just another example of health care $ bloat from bad insurance practices.

@UHC announces they’re going to cut prior authorization off 30% of medical services…call me a skeptic, but I think time will tell if they’re just cutting administrative burden on the front end to shift towards financial denials on the backend, which are even harder to identify and subsequently appeal.

Will denials go up? Downcodes? What about retrospective medical necessity review (healthcare already performed, and then after the fact declared to not have medical necessity) or coverage exclusions?

A current 92% prior authorization approval rate means that we already know prior auth is just annoying administrative burden…but the real answer of how impactful this is will lay in the denials rate…

🤔
